lines.text: Right. You came up here after work and there's work going, so you're taken on. The pay is poor and the walking is most of it, and there's more ground out there than one person gets round in a season.
My name's Maren. Warden for the region, and it's been the one post since they made it.
There was a keystone animal here once. The Vellsire, a stag. The last of that herd went out of Fallowmere about thirty years back, and the ground up here has been without them ever since.

Three in the pen behind you. A Cindril, a Puddlisk and a Thornlet, all of them out of this spring. A young one has about three years of work in it, and after that it comes back here and lives on without working.
Have a proper look at all three, because I can't swap it over afterwards.
The Cindril, then. Fire animal, and the quickest of the three by a long way.
It'll be a Vulkindle at two and a Pyrevane at three. Same animal the whole way through with a new name on it each time. Bring it down when it changes and I'll weigh it.
The Puddlisk, then. Water animal.

The skin's clear enough to watch its dinner go down inside it. Rillisk at two, Maelstrisk at three, and they go over in the night, so you come down to something bigger with a different name on the card.
The Thornlet, then. Plant animal, and it'll open your forearm up if you carry it against your chest, so use the crook of your arm. Bramblore at two, Thornwald at three.
Same animal each time, only bigger. By the third year you'll not lift it.
Snares first. Three of them, in the satchel by the door. The satchel comes back to me.

One snare holds one animal long enough for you to get your hands on it, and after that there's one fewer where you took it from. Bait makes a snare likelier to hold, and you make the bait out of whatever the animal eats.
A base one lets go of anything that fights hard. A weighted one holds, and the smith sends them up when he has the iron for it. Keep the weighted for whatever's already put a team down.
And this is the survey board. Every place in the region down one side, what's living in it written against the place, and a number against that.
Most of what's on it is mine, which is the reason it reads three weeks out of date anywhere north of the gate, and further behind than that up on the steppe.
So read it on your way out the north gate and again coming back. Take four of the Nibbin off Meadow Reach and the board reads four fewer when I write it up that evening.
One more thing before you go far. There'll be tracks out on the Reach, and droppings, and a flattened patch where something's lain up. Read one and you'll know what came past and roughly when.
Some things are only here part of the year. Pollywisp are a spring animal on the Reach, so a card read on one in autumn comes back dormant. And a dull animal reads nothing off a good clear track.
Walk Meadow Reach and write me three cards.
Three cards. A Loamunder, a Nibbin, and one you weren't sure of. I'd put that down as Bramblehog.
Three more than I had for the Reach at the start of the week. There's a word you'll want off me before you go much further and it's keystone. Ask me for it at the station any morning this week.
One more thing about the snares. They work the other way round as well, which is the half people don't get told. You can open one and let the animal back out.
Whatever you let out goes into the ground or the water you're standing on.

Not back where you caught it. A release goes on the board the same way a catch does, only the number goes up instead of down. Hetty has wanted somebody putting Boglings back since spring. Go and see her.
The green's holding up out on the Reach this year.

I'd put a fair bit of that down to the Loamunder turning the soil as they go, and that's a guess, mind. Maribel keeps the gym at the bottom of the green, and it's the old Nibbin that'll give you trouble.
Odo has the gym out on the east stilts. Three weeks since I was over at Brackmarsh, and it rained every day of it, so what I've got written for that marsh is short of what's in it.
The silk and the timber come off the same trees here, and the two trades want different things off them. Vesper keeps the gym, and she's on the council over exactly that.
Gerta has the steppe survey and she can't walk the whole of it on her own, which is the reason I'm asking. She's at the third shaft head most mornings and below all week.
Orrin's shelves go back further than anything I keep, and I've been up there every morning this week instead of walking the vale. He'll read the whole page out to you if you let him.
The gate is standing open. It has not been open in my lifetime and it was not me that opened it. The crows on this approach want counting before noon and I've not started.
You asked what a keystone is.
It's an animal a great many other things turn out to depend on, far more than you'd guess from how few there are. Take one out and everything shifts about after it, slowly.

Some go up, some go down, and none of it shows on paper for four seasons. Where the Vellsire herd grazed, the ground came back richer the next year, and three people who didn't know each other wrote that down separately.
You read one of the stones out on the Reach. There are more.
I've walked to three of the others myself this season. The rest I have off Orrin, who has them off a surveyor's letter, and I'd want to walk them before I said anything about them.
Whoever cut them was keeping a tally. The ones that still have a face carry the same six figures. The herd has not passed in thirty years and the stones go back a good deal further than that.
The felling crews let me at a fresh stump when I ask, and I've had forty-odd off them. You can read a tree's years off a stump: a wide ring is a fat year, a thin one is a poor year.
Every one of those forty reads wide, wide, wide, and then thin to the bark.

The thin starts within a season of the last time anybody wrote down seeing a Vellsire. One stump like that is a bad tree. Forty like that and I still can't call it anything, and I'd rather say so than guess.
I've not been up that steppe since the thaw. Anything I tell you about it is Gerta's work.

There's less green up there than on the Reach. A place empties from the bottom up. Green goes first, then whatever lived on the green. Whatever was at the top goes last, and it has been hungry a long while by then.
Four days I've been up at Orrin's shelves, and what I wanted off them was not the total.
I wanted to know who took each entry and where they were standing, and thirty years of those nights carry nothing in the margin at all.

Not one of those hands put down the hour, or the weather, or whether they went out looking or just happened to be at the window. I can use figures like that. Putting a season on them is another matter.
The Sanctum Fallow was shut before those stones were cut. Fallow is a farming word and it means ground you've left to rest on purpose, so somebody shut it and meant it to come back.
If the herd went anywhere it went in there.

There'll be no herd left to find, though. One animal at the outside, and an old one. What you do standing in front of it is yours to decide, and it'll be a long while before it shows in anything I can measure.
The animal's out of working years. It's come to the end of what it had in it, and there's nothing wrong with it otherwise.

Two things can come of this. Either a young one out of the same stock carrying one or two of the things this one was good at, or something you've already got gets better at one thing for good, in this one's name.
It'll be down at the station from tomorrow, fed, with the run of the yard and no work at all for the rest of its life. The yard gets fed at four, same as it always has.
The west scarp has carried three big Stonewing every year I've had this job. Gerta walked it five days back and found one.

I can't tell you yet what took them off. If it's gone the usual way, the Cragmar and the Ashvole thinned out first, then the Pyrelisk that feed on the Ashvole, and a bird that size feels it last of all.
Greaves went through the gate about an hour ago, on foot, and he did not hurry any part of it.
I'll be up on the rim with the board. There's a morning's work still on it and I'd like it done before the light goes.
You've got the stag, then. Let me look at it a minute. It's narrower through the shoulder than the drawings have it, and the near antler's been broken and grown back crooked. It won't age.
Right. The numbers, then. Meadow Reach, Brackmarsh, Bowerdeep Wilds, Cinder Steppe, Duskhollow Vale and the Approach, all six walked and counted this morning. Five by me and the steppe by Gerta.

With that animal held, the ground round the Sanctum and along the Approach holds at the rate it has held every year I've walked it: two young brought on, where three is what it makes with the stag loose in there.
I'll put in the book that the snare held and what was in it, and the six figures under it, with Gerta's name against the steppe one.
The stag went up the scarp and over the rim and out of sight. It stopped the once at the top, side on, long enough for me to see all of it. I had a pencil in my hand and never wrote a thing down.
Right. The numbers, then. Meadow Reach, Brackmarsh, Bowerdeep Wilds, Cinder Steppe, Duskhollow Vale and the Approach, all six walked and counted this morning. Five by me and the steppe by Gerta.
With that animal loose, the ground round the Sanctum and along the Approach comes off that rate for the first time: three young brought on, where two is what it has always made.
You were six years getting to it. In nine years somebody will ask me why the numbers moved, and I'd rather they had all of it from me.
Station's open, come in. This morning's numbers are up on the board, and the Reach column is the only one I've walked this week. The rest are last month's and I've marked them as last month's.
The board goes under one arm and I'm out along the stilts most days this season. Four hours out of a day is what I get before the damp's into the pages.
Bowerdeep is slow ground for me. I'm on the forest floor with a glass looking up. That gets me about a third of the canopy, and I write the third down and mark it as a third.
Steppe survey, and I'm behind on it. Read over my shoulder if you like.
Shelves in the morning, out in the vale from dusk, because that's when the things I'm after are up and moving, which gives me about four hours before the light comes back.
I'm up at the rim most of the day with the board. Crows are the only thing living on this approach, and they're what I'm counting.
